before: A Conditional Propellant Estimate for Shipboard Booster Recovery: Trajectory Optimization, Attitude Feasibility, and Safety Limits
after: A Conditional Propellant Estimate for Shipboard Booster Recovery: Translational Optimization and Attitude Constraints

before: This paper addresses the problem of estimating the propellant required for a first-stage booster that separates at an altitude of 70 km with a speed of 6,000 km/h and a dry mass of 130 t and must be recovered on a ship. Because the initial flight-path angle, propulsion performance, aerodynamics, and actuator limits are unspecified, the problem does not determine a unique propellant load. We therefore develop a staged model that separates a transparent translational reference model from the attitude, contact, and safety checks required to interpret its result, and we evaluate an explicitly horizontal, wind-free reference scenario under spherical gravity, standard atmospheric density, variable mass, constant drag coefficient 0.5, and a virtual three-engine propulsion system with specific impulse 320 s.
after: We estimate the propellant required to recover a first-stage booster that separates at 70 km altitude with a speed of 6,000 km/h and a dry mass of 130 t. The unspecified velocity direction, engine performance, aerodynamics, and landing hardware preclude a unique real-vehicle estimate. We therefore define a horizontal, wind-free reference scenario with spherical gravity, standard atmospheric density, variable mass, a constant drag coefficient of 0.5, and three virtual engines with a specific impulse of 320 s.

before: Direct multiple shooting identifies a nominal trajectory carrying approximately 149 t of liquid oxygen and methane and consuming approximately 148 t before a center-of-gravity reference endpoint. The selected strategy coasts for 40 s, performs a three-engine entry burn, and restarts two engines for the final burn. Independent integration gives a flight time of 218 s, a nominal ship range of 206 km, a peak dynamic pressure of 47.0 kPa, and a reference descent speed of 1.00 m/s. Attitude analysis reveals that a net thrust-to-body deflection of at least 24.8 degrees is required at one high-pressure instant, and nine deterministic perturbations fail the unchanged open-loop plan.
after: Direct multiple shooting yields a nominal candidate carrying 149.30 t of liquid oxygen and methane and consuming 147.84 t before reaching a center-of-gravity reference endpoint. The sequence comprises a 40 s coast, a three-engine entry burn, and a two-engine final burn. Independent integration gives a flight time of 217.75 s, a downrange distance of 206.35 km, a peak dynamic pressure of 47.01 kPa, and a reference descent speed of approximately 1.00 m/s. However, retaining this trajectory under the assumed high-pressure inflow constraint requires at least 24.8° of net thrust-to-body deflection at one instant. All nine deterministic perturbations fail the unchanged open-loop plan.

before: We therefore report the propellant value as a reproducible nominal research candidate rather than a certified safe load or a global minimum. The principal contribution is the set of attitude, contact, and safety checks — supported by independent numerical verification — that makes the conditional status of the result explicit and that defines precisely what must still be established before a safe-landing propellant requirement can be certified.
after: The 149 t value is consequently a reproducible translational benchmark, not a demonstrated safe-landing load or a global minimum. The analysis identifies the attitude, foot-contact, deck-coverage, and post-contact conditions that must be resolved before a complete recovery estimate can be justified.

before: Keywords: Booster recovery; trajectory optimization; propellant estimation; attitude feasibility; foot-contact safety; numerical verification; optimal control; direct multiple shooting
after: Keywords: booster recovery; propellant estimation; trajectory optimization; attitude constraints; foot contact; numerical verification

before: Recovering a booster requires more than reducing its center-of-gravity speed. The vehicle must survive atmospheric entry, reach a fixed finite deck, orient its body, control both feet or all deployed supports at first contact, and remain stable while its engines shut down. The problem specifies the separation altitude, speed, dry mass, dimensions, and propellant species, and allows the ship to be placed conveniently [1]. It does not specify the initial velocity direction, engine performance, aerodynamic coefficients, body orientation, landing-gear properties, or allowable heating and structural loads.
after: Recovery requires the booster to withstand atmospheric entry, reach a fixed finite deck, approach with an acceptable body attitude, and remain stable during contact and engine shutdown. The problem specifies separation altitude and speed, dry mass, vehicle dimensions, and propellant species, while allowing the ship to be positioned conveniently [1]. It leaves the initial velocity direction, propulsion performance, aerodynamic coefficients, attitude-control capability, landing-gear properties, and allowable structural and thermal loads unspecified.

before: This underdetermination is the central difficulty of the problem. A propellant estimate that is meaningful for a real vehicle cannot be obtained by silently assuming the very specifications that are missing; it must instead be conditional — valid for a transparent reference scenario and accompanied by an explicit statement of which additional inputs would be required to certify it. The fundamental question this paper addresses can be articulated as follows: what propellant value can be defended from the given information, and which attitude, contact, and safety conditions must still be established before that value can be treated as a safe-load certificate?
after: We therefore seek a conditional estimate: a propellant load for a stated reference model, together with an assessment of whether that trajectory can meet additional recovery requirements. This distinction allows a numerical answer without treating assumed hardware properties as established facts.

before: We address this underdetermination by separating three questions. First, what trajectories are possible in a transparent translational reference model? Second, how much initial propellant does a low-consumption candidate in a restricted strategy family carry? Third, can that candidate satisfy additional attitude and landing requirements? We denote the translational model M0. A coupled rigid-body, actuator, and contact model is denoted M1; only its governing relations and necessary feasibility conditions are developed here, not a completed M1 landing simulation.
after: The study separates trajectory generation from recovery feasibility. Model M0 describes variable-mass translation and provides a low-consumption candidate within a restricted strategy family. Model M1 denotes the coupled translation, rotation, actuator, and contact problem needed to assess recovery. This paper develops necessary conditions and governing relations for M1 but does not solve a complete M1 landing simulation.

before: Translational reference trajectory. Develop a variable-mass, point-mass model M0 in a vertical great-circle plane, and search a restricted schedule family for a low-consumption nominal trajectory by direct multiple shooting.
after: Translational model: formulate M0 in a vertical great-circle plane and search a restricted burn sequence using direct multiple shooting.

before: Independent numerical verification. Replay the nominal schedule with independently written coordinate systems and integrators to establish that the reported trajectory is reproducible, not an artifact of a single solver configuration.
after: Numerical verification: check the nominal result with independently written coordinate formulations and integrators.

before: Attitude feasibility. Derive the necessary thrust-to-body deflection conditions that the reference trajectory imposes, and use them to falsify any claim that a prescribed thrust direction is automatically realizable.
after: Attitude assessment: determine whether the required thrust direction is compatible with assumed body-angle and deflection limits.

before: Safety framework. Enumerate the contact, deck-coverage, structural, and thermal criteria (C01–C18) and identify, criterion by criterion, which remain unverified.
after: Recovery assessment: distinguish the implemented M0 checks from the unresolved attitude, contact, deck, structural, and thermal requirements. The safety list comprises 18 classes and 19 records, with C13 split into C13a and C13b.

before: The scope is deliberately bounded. The principal result is conditional: approximately 149 t is a reproducible M0 candidate under the stated assumptions, not an unconditional answer for an unspecified real booster. The safety analysis supplies concrete reasons for this distinction rather than assuming that attitude control will automatically realize a prescribed thrust vector.
after: The principal numerical result is an approximately 149 t M0 candidate. Its reproducibility is assessed separately from its physical feasibility: neither a prescribed thrust direction nor a low center-of-gravity speed establishes safe foot contact.

before: The work proceeds through four stages. First, we classify every input as given by the problem, drawn from literature, chosen as a scenario assumption, or not established (Section 2), and we run passive diagnostics that establish which physical effects must be retained (Section 3). Second, we assemble the variable-mass translational model and its propellant and engine-response accounting (Section 4), and we search a restricted low-consumption schedule family with an independently replayed numerical method (Section 5). Third, we extract the nominal trajectory and propellant result (Section 6) and subject it to grid, coordinate, and integrator verification together with nine deterministic perturbations (Section 7). Fourth, we develop the attitude feasibility conditions (Section 8) and the foot-contact, deck-coverage, and post-contact safety checks (Section 9), and we assemble the resulting strengths, limitations, and completion path (Section 10) before concluding (Section 11).
after: We first state the input assumptions and examine passive trajectories (Sections 2–3). We then formulate and solve the translational problem and independently verify its nominal result (Sections 4–7). Finally, we assess necessary attitude conditions and contact geometry, identify unresolved recovery requirements, and discuss their implications for the propellant estimate (Sections 8–11).

before: The engine family is deliberately virtual; no named production engine is claimed to have these combined properties. There are three installed engines, each with reference thrust 1 MN and steady normalized throttle between 0.3 and 1.1. The last continuous burn uses two engines as a reference scheduling choice, not an optimality theorem. One engine at maximum thrust cannot provide positive low-speed vertical acceleration against even the dry weight, since 1.1 MN < 130000 g₀ ≈ 1.275 MN. Two engines span 0.6–2.2 MN and have a dry-mass hovering throttle near 0.64. Three engines can also hover because their minimum total thrust, 0.9 MN, is below the dry weight; they are not excluded on that basis.
after: The propulsion system is a virtual three-engine model. Each engine has a reference thrust of 1 MN and a steady throttle range of 0.3–1.1. Two engines are used for the final burn as a scheduling choice, not as a proven optimum. At low speed, one engine cannot provide upward acceleration against even the dry weight because 1.1 MN < 130000 g₀ ≈ 1.275 MN. Two engines span 0.6–2.2 MN, with a dry-mass hovering throttle near 0.64. Three engines can also hover because their minimum combined thrust is 0.9 MN; their exclusion from the final burn is not a feasibility result.

before: The baseline motion lies in a vertical great-circle plane. Earth is spherical and non-rotating, the atmosphere is at rest, and the ship is fixed after its nominal position is selected. The separation velocity is horizontal, so vt,0 = 1666.667 m s⁻¹ and vr,0 = 0. These are scenario assumptions, not consequences of the stated speed. An initially upward trajectory may exceed the 70 km density domain used here and requires an extended atmosphere model before further computation.
after: The reference motion lies in a vertical great-circle plane over a spherical, non-rotating Earth. The atmosphere is stationary, and the ship remains fixed after its nominal location is selected. Horizontal separation gives vt,0 = 1666.667 m/s and vr,0 = 0. These are scenario assumptions; the specified speed alone does not determine them. An upward initial trajectory may leave the implemented 0–70 km atmospheric domain and would require that domain to be extended.

before: This paper makes the following contributions to the modeling of underdetermined launch-vehicle recovery problems:
after: The study combines four elements:

before: Evidence-status classification. An explicit G/L/H/U framework separates quantities given by the problem, literature constants, scenario assumptions, and unestablished inputs, so that the conditional nature of the propellant estimate is stated rather than hidden.
after: Input classification: the G/L/H/U labels distinguish problem data, literature references, scenario assumptions, and unresolved inputs.

before: Reproducible low-consumption trajectory. A variable-mass translational (M0) trajectory obtained by direct multiple shooting and accepted only after independent coordinate, integrator, and grid-convergence checks.
after: Traceable computation: the M0 candidate is accompanied by independent replay, coordinate comparisons, and a control-grid refinement study.

before: Attitude falsification. Necessary thrust-to-body deflection conditions that demonstrate the reference trajectory is not automatically realizable and that falsify overly strong safety claims.
after: A necessary attitude test: thrust and body-angle intervals identify incompatibilities that are invisible in a point-mass trajectory.

before: Enumerated safety boundary. A criterion-by-criterion (C01–C18) accounting of foot contact, deck coverage, structure, and heating that identifies exactly which evidence remains missing before a safe-landing certificate can be issued.
after: An explicit recovery checklist: the 18 safety classes distinguish nominal M0 results from missing attitude, contact, structural, and thermal evidence. These are elements of the present analysis, not claims of new optimization algorithms or general safety theory.

before: Before assembling the full model, we establish which physical effects cannot be neglected for a trajectory of this scale. At separation, h₀/R = 0.0110 and g(h₀) = 9.61 m s⁻², compared with g(0) = 9.82 m s⁻². The curvature acceleration V₀²/(R + h₀) ≈ 0.431 m s⁻² is not negligible for a trajectory extending roughly 200 km. The initial specific kinetic energy is 1.39 MJ kg⁻¹, while the gravitational potential decrease to sea level is about 0.680 MJ kg⁻¹. Thus gravity affects both the terminal velocity and the duration of powered braking. A constant-mass approximation is especially inappropriate once the candidate propellant mass is comparable to the dry mass.
after: Several effects are significant at the stated scale. At separation, h₀/R = 0.0110 and g(h₀) = 9.61 m/s², compared with g(0) = 9.82 m/s². The curvature term V₀²/(R + h₀) ≈ 0.431 m/s² affects a trajectory extending roughly 200 km. Initial specific kinetic energy is 1.39 MJ/kg, while the gravitational potential decrease to sea level is about 0.680 MJ/kg. Gravity and curvature are therefore retained. A constant-mass approximation is also unsuitable when the candidate propellant load is comparable to the dry mass.

before: Even the higher-drag passive case reaches the surface at hundreds of meters per second and exceeds the assumed 50 kPa screening target. Atmospheric drag therefore helps but does not establish soft landing. These calculations also show why a sea-level terminal-velocity estimate is not a complete impact-speed prediction: the vehicle may not have enough path length to approach that asymptotic speed.
after: Both atmospheric cases reach the surface at hundreds of meters per second and exceed the assumed 50 kPa screening limit. Drag reduces the braking requirement but does not produce a soft landing. A sea-level terminal-speed estimate is insufficient because the body descends through changing density and may not approach its local terminal speed before impact.

before: The horizontal component in the local tangent direction consequently rises to approximately 1,685 m/s at the surface in the horizontal-separation diagnostic. Gravity is conservative and does not dissipate the initial horizontal momentum. The convenient-ship provision avoids an imposed return-to-launch-site maneuver; it does not eliminate the need for terminal horizontal braking. Drag and engine thrust supply the actual dissipative or controlled changes.
after: The local tangential speed therefore increases to approximately 1,685 m/s at the surface in this vacuum diagnostic. Central gravity changes the velocity direction and its local components but exerts no torque about Earth’s center. Allowing a downrange ship avoids a return-to-launch-site requirement; it does not remove the horizontal-braking requirement. In the controlled trajectory, drag and appropriately directed thrust change the angular momentum.

before: We select the ship once at the nominal controlled downrange location. In perturbation tests the nominal ship is not moved to follow a changed endpoint. The approximately 199–202 km passive ranges above and the approximately 206 km controlled range need not agree, since thrust alters the trajectory.
after: The ship is placed once at the nominal controlled endpoint and is not moved in perturbation tests. The passive ranges of approximately 199–202 km need not match the controlled range of approximately 206 km, because thrust changes the flight path.

before: Earth constants are supported by [3,4]. The constant C_D = 0.5 and zero lift are scenario choices. Drag depends on shape, orientation, and flow conditions [6], so this closure is not a measured aerodynamic database. Retropropulsion experiments also demonstrate dependence on thrust and vehicle configuration [10]; their coefficients are not transferred to this different booster.
after: The Earth constants are taken from [3,4]. The constant drag coefficient C_D = 0.5 and zero lift are assumptions, not a measured aerodynamic database. Drag depends on vehicle shape, orientation, and flow conditions [6]. Retropropulsion experiments also show configuration- and thrust-dependent flow [10]; their measured coefficients are not applied to this different booster.

before: The drag contribution is interpreted as zero when V = 0. Here all active thrust vectors are parallel, so T equals the sum of engine thrust magnitudes. Specific impulse relates thrust to total propellant mass flow [5]. In a later nonparallel allocation, the vector sum must be used for translation, whereas the sum of thrust magnitudes determines mass flow and the force budget.
after: The drag term is defined as zero at V = 0. All active M0 thrust vectors are parallel, so T is both their resultant magnitude and the sum of individual thrust magnitudes. The mass-flow relation uses constant specific impulse [5]. If a later model allows nonparallel engine vectors, translation must use their vector sum, while propellant flow depends on the sum of engine thrust magnitudes.

before: Unusable residue is carried as mass and cannot be burned. The nominal usable reserve target is mres = 2.2×10⁶/(320 g₀) = 701.055 kg, equivalent to one second of maximum two-engine thrust. A further 10 kg numerical buffer is imposed during optimization. This is an H reserve definition, not demonstrated disturbance tolerance.
after: The unusable fraction remains part of the vehicle mass but cannot be consumed. The usable reserve target is mres = 2.2×10⁶/(320 g₀) = 701.055 kg, corresponding to one second of maximum two-engine thrust. Optimization includes a further 10 kg buffer. This is a nominal bookkeeping requirement, not a demonstrated allowance for disturbances or emergency maneuvers.

before: During controlled burn segments, actual throttle is piecewise linear. Its implied effective command is ucmd = u + 0.1 u̇, constrained between 0.3 and 1.1 at both ends of each segment. Startup and shutdown may pass below 0.3; that bound applies to steady powered operation. Shutdown includes the corresponding rate-limited decrease and exponential tail. No extra shutdown-command delay has been established, so it is not silently assumed in the contact discussion.
after: During controlled burn segments, actual throttle is piecewise linear. The implied command ucmd = u + 0.1 u̇ is constrained to 0.3–1.1 at both ends of each segment, and the throttle slew limit is checked separately. Startup and shutdown may pass below 0.3 because the lower bound applies only to steady powered operation. Shutdown includes a rate-limited decrease followed by an exponential tail. No additional shutdown-command delay is assumed.

before: over a specified schedule family: initial coast; three-engine entry burn; an off command; a two-engine restart command five seconds later; and a final two-engine burn. The five seconds separate commands and are not a full zero-thrust interval. Engine response accounts for the 0.5 s restart delay and subsequent buildup. The landing pair ignites twice, while the third engine ignites once, below the assumed three-ignition limit per engine.
after: The strategy family consists of an initial coast, a three-engine entry burn, an off command, a two-engine restart command five seconds later, and a final two-engine burn. The five-second interval separates commands; shutdown and restart dynamics prevent it from being a full zero-thrust interval. The landing pair ignites twice and the third engine once, within the assumed limit of three ignitions per engine.

before: The endpoint is a center-of-gravity reference event, not actual foot contact:
after: The terminal target is a center-of-gravity reference state, not a foot-contact condition:

before: The optimized vertical endpoint thrust is at most 0.95 times local weight. Replay checks that vertical thrust at the independently detected reference event does not exceed weight. This does not prove support stability after contact.
after: The optimization limits terminal vertical thrust to 0.95 times local weight. At the independently detected reference event, replay checks that vertical thrust does not exceed weight. Neither condition demonstrates stable support after actual contact.

before: We use direct multiple shooting with CasADi [7] and the local interior-point solver IPOPT [8]. Each powered phase is divided into 80, 160, and then 320 control intervals, using four RK4 substeps per interval. Coast steps are no longer than 0.5 s; startup uses 64 steps of 0.025 s; the shutdown/restart transition uses 132 steps of 0.05 s with actual midpoint response values.
after: Direct multiple shooting is implemented with CasADi [7] and IPOPT [8]. Each powered phase is successively discretized into 80, 160, and 320 control intervals, with four RK4 substeps per interval. Coast steps are at most 0.5 s; startup uses 64 steps of 0.025 s; and the shutdown/restart transition uses 132 steps of 0.05 s with the actual response evaluated at the midpoint.

before: Optimization success alone is not acceptance. Some bounds are imposed only at control nodes or RK substeps; the initial coast/startup do not carry every path constraint in the optimizer. We therefore replay the complete schedule with independent SI Cartesian equations, DOP853, explicit control breakpoints, and a continuous reference-altitude event [9]. Maximum-step halving, 0.05 s sampling, and local peak refinement screen the nominal path. A separately written SI polar model and RK45 provide further checks. This is strong numerical evidence, not an analytic continuous-time safety proof or a global optimum certificate.
after: Solver convergence is followed by independent replay. Because some optimizer bounds are enforced only at control nodes or RK substeps, and not all path constraints are imposed during coast and startup, the complete schedule is reintegrated in SI Cartesian coordinates with DOP853, explicit control breakpoints, and a continuous reference-altitude event [9]. A 0.05 s sample spacing, maximum-step halving, and local peak refinement check the nominal path. An independently written SI polar model and RK45 provide additional comparisons. These checks establish numerical consistency for this candidate; they do not prove continuous-time constraint satisfaction analytically or global optimality.

before: The fixed 40 s initial coast provides the lowest accepted load among the tested cases. The 20, 40, and 50 s preliminary comparisons use 80 intervals per powered phase; the final 40 s candidate is refined to 320 intervals. The immediately ignited reference is also evaluated at 320 intervals. The refined 40 s candidate carries 1.56 t less than the immediate-ignition reference, approximately 1.04%. These comparisons are within the chosen model and schedule family. Failed fixed-load schedules or failed solver runs are not universal lower bounds on the required fuel.
after: The 40 s initial-coast case gives the lowest accepted load in the tested family. Preliminary 20, 40, and 50 s cases use 80 intervals per powered phase; the selected 40 s case and the immediate-ignition reference are evaluated at 320 intervals. The refined 40 s candidate carries 1.56 t less propellant than the immediate-ignition reference, a reduction of approximately 1.04%. The mixed-resolution preliminary comparison is not a converged ranking of every ignition time. Failed solver runs or fixed-load schedules do not establish a universal lower bound.

before: The second burn begins while substantial horizontal and vertical velocities remain; it is not a purely vertical final braking pulse. The nominal ship is selected at the computed surface arc range; no geographical coordinates can be inferred without a launch location and heading.
after: At the two-engine restart, substantial tangential and radial velocities remain, so the final burn is not a purely vertical braking maneuver. The ship is selected at the nominal surface-arc range. A geographical landing location would also require the separation location and heading.

before: The initial total mass is 279.30 t. The 149.30 t propellant load contains approximately 115.37 t oxygen and 33.93 t methane if the assumed oxidizer-to-fuel mass ratio is 3.4. At the reference endpoint, approximately 1.458 t of propellant remains: 0.746 t unusable residue and 0.711 t usable reserve. The actual consumed total, about 147.84 t, must not be confused with the initial load or methane alone.
after: Initial total mass is 279.30 t. With an assumed oxygen-to-methane mass ratio of 3.4, the 149.30 t load comprises approximately 115.37 t oxygen and 33.93 t methane. At the reference endpoint, about 1.458 t remains: 0.746 t unusable residue and 0.711 t usable reserve, with the difference attributable to rounding. The 147.84 t consumed mass is total propellant, not methane alone.

before: This scalar thrust increment includes the effort required along the powered trajectory; it is not simply the passive impact speed. Finite burn duration, gravity, changing mass, and direction changes matter. A rocket-equation estimate that inserts a chosen terminal speed while fixing the acceleration at near-dry mass does not close this coupled problem. The relatively large load is consistent with a low-thrust, long-duration braking history constrained to avoid high dynamic pressure; it is not an established universal minimum.
after: This scalar characteristic velocity is the integral of thrust acceleration magnitude, not the net velocity change or passive impact speed. It incorporates the thrust expended along a changing flight path. Estimating it from an assumed impact speed and a near-dry-mass braking acceleration would neglect the coupled evolution of mass, gravity, drag, and thrust direction. The relatively large load is consistent with the candidate’s long powered descent under the imposed dynamic-pressure limit; it is not a universal minimum.

before: The 160-to-320 interval propellant change is 0.0189%, and independent reference-speed differences are much smaller than the modeled physical uncertainties. Re-solving the 320-interval problem from the archived 160-interval initial guess reproduces the final mass, times, and state/control nodes. This tests the same local solution path, not multiple-basin or global optimality.
after: Refining from 160 to 320 intervals changes the initial propellant load by 0.0189%. This is evidence of local grid refinement, not a proven error bound. Re-solving the 320-interval problem from the archived 160-interval guess reproduces the reported mass, timing, and state/control nodes. The coordinate and integrator comparisons in Table 7 further support numerical reproducibility, but none tests global optimality or uncertainty in the assumed physics.

before: Input validation matters as well as integration accuracy. An earlier replay could accept raw thrust-angle values shifted by 2π, because the forces are periodic and the raw angle bounds were not explicitly rechecked. The delivered nominal angles are within bounds. A stricter validator now rejects angle-range violations, nonfinite throttle values, wrong array shapes, and invalid timing before replay. This fixes an acceptance-interface gap without changing the nominal trajectory.
after: The replay input validator explicitly rejects out-of-range thrust angles, nonfinite throttle values, incorrect array shapes, and invalid timing. This is necessary because angles shifted by 2π can produce identical forces while violating raw control bounds. The nominal controls satisfy the strengthened validation checks.

before: Each case below keeps the initial propellant mass and the full control schedule fixed and changes one parameter. The nominal ship location is fixed. Integration ends at reference contact, usable-propellant exhaustion, or the original planned final time; the control is not extended into an undefined landing maneuver. The reserve threshold remains its fixed nominal definition. The Isp test changes mass flow without inventing a simultaneous thrust-performance map.
after: Each test changes one parameter while keeping initial propellant, control history, and ship location fixed. Integration stops at the CG reference event, usable-propellant exhaustion, or the original planned final time. Controls are not extended beyond their defined interval. The reserve threshold keeps its nominal value. Changing Isp changes mass flow only in this test; it does not introduce an unprovided thrust-performance map.

before: All nine tests fail the original reference plan, even before full attitude and contact safety are assessed. A 1 m/s decrease in initial tangential speed, only about 0.06% of the nominal speed, produces an 11.5 m/s reference descent speed. A 1% lower specific impulse exhausts usable propellant at a CG height near 300 m. The nominal reserve is only about 10 kg above its stated 701 kg threshold; satisfying that bookkeeping requirement does not establish robustness.
after: None of the nine perturbed cases passes the original M0 acceptance checks. A 1 m/s reduction in initial tangential speed, approximately 0.06% of the nominal speed, gives an 11.5 m/s descent speed at the CG reference event. Reducing specific impulse by 1% exhausts usable propellant near 300 m altitude. These failures occur before complete attitude and foot-contact checks. The nominal reserve exceeds its 701 kg target by only about 10 kg; this bookkeeping margin does not establish robustness.

before: Failure to contact by the planned time does not mean that later controlled landing is impossible. Likewise, these results do not show that a redesigned feedback controller would fail. They demonstrate the sensitivity of this fixed open-loop schedule. The nine cases are not random samples and provide neither a failure probability nor a propellant confidence interval. Selected drag, specific-impulse, and initial-speed cases were repeated with RK45; event categories agree and endpoint height/velocity differences are below 0.01 in the corresponding SI units.
after: A case that has not reached the reference height by the planned end time may still admit a different controlled landing. The tests assess sensitivity of one fixed open-loop schedule, not the capability of a redesigned feedback controller. They are deterministic cases, so they provide neither a failure probability nor a confidence interval for propellant. Selected drag, specific-impulse, and initial-speed cases were repeated with RK45; event categories agree, and endpoint differences remain below 0.01 m in height and 0.01 m/s in velocity.

before: The high-pressure inflow screen requires the body axis to lie within 5 degrees of the direction opposite relative velocity when descending at q ≥ 10 kPa. The late descent screen requires body tilt within 5 degrees once the lowest deployed-foot clearance is at most 200 m. The assumed first-contact limits are 2 degrees body tilt and 0.5 degrees/s relative body angular rate. None is automatically enforced by a thrust-direction trace.
after: The assumed high-pressure inflow limit requires the body axis to remain within 5° of the direction opposite relative velocity during descent at q ≥ 10 kPa. A separate late-descent limit requires body tilt within 5° when the lowest deployed-foot clearance is at most 200 m. First-contact limits are 2° body tilt and 0.5°/s angular rate relative to the deck. These constrain body motion, not merely the prescribed thrust direction.

before: This is a necessary lower bound for keeping the existing trajectory. If the available net deflection is at most 20 degrees, no body angle at that instant can satisfy both requirements. Near the ground, the analogous required relative deflection is about 15.28 degrees under the local-deck approximation. The actual actuator capability is unknown; the numbers are requirements, not specifications.
after: This is a necessary instantaneous lower bound for retaining the M0 trajectory. A net deflection limit of 20° or less makes the inflow and thrust requirements incompatible at that instant. Near the ground, the analogous bound is approximately 15.28° using the local-deck approximation. These are trajectory-dependent requirements, not established actuator specifications.

before: A sweep of assumed net deflection limits 3, 5, 10, 15, and 20 degrees finds incompatible instants. At 25 and 30 degrees, the samples have no instantaneous angle contradiction. Even then, torque, rate, initial orientation, and a continuous dynamically achievable body trajectory remain unverified.
after: For assumed net deflection limits of 3°, 5°, 10°, 15°, and 20°, the sampled angle intervals are incompatible at some instants. Limits of 25° and 30° remove this sampled instantaneous contradiction, but do not establish a continuous body trajectory with feasible torque, angular rate, or initial attitude.

Both Cm and pressure-center location are unknown. A changing center of mass and inertia require a consistent control-volume angular-momentum balance, including relevant mass-flow transport terms; an arbitrary time-varying inertia cannot be inserted while ignoring the corresponding terms.
after: The moment sign follows from the clockwise angle convention. Aerodynamic moment may be represented by qArefL Cm or by an aerodynamic force applied at a pressure center; neither Cm nor that location is established here. Equation (13) must not be used as a complete variable-mass attitude equation by inserting an arbitrary I(t) and omitting the corresponding transport terms.

before: Actual first contact is the earliest continuous zero of a deployed-foot clearance, provided the non-supporting envelope has not touched first. The main-cylinder proxy occupies s ∈ [2, 65] m with radius 3.5 m; both sides are sampled every 1 m and joined as a closed polygon. At foot contact and |θd| < 90°, its minimum clearance is 2 cos θd + (b − 3.5)|sin θd| > 0. The 2 m basal gap and 5 m deployed half-span are assumptions, not a measured layout. after: At 2° tilt, the lowest foot contacts a flat deck when Hc ≈ 32.655 m, while the other foot is approximately 2b|sin 2°| = 0.349 m higher. Load transfer is therefore generally nonsimultaneous. before: A spherical flight model also needs consistent local deck coordinates. Far from the ship, ocean clearance is measured from the spherical sea surface; an infinite extension of the ship's tangent plane is not the global ocean. Segment interiors must be tested for minimum distance to the sphere, not just vertices. Near the ship, finite deck and hull geometry replace the infinite-plane approximation.
after: Contact geometry must be consistent with the spherical flight model. Away from the ship, clearance is measured relative to the spherical sea surface, not an infinite extension of the ship’s tangent plane. A polygonal envelope requires minimum-distance checks along segment interiors as well as vertices. Near the ship, the finite deck and hull geometry determine contact.

after: Let B be the foot-plane center. The target-error condition is |xB − xship| ≤ 5 m (C13a). before: At reference mass 131.46 t, vertical kinetic energy is approximately 65.7 kJ at 1 m/s and 263 kJ at 2 m/s. after: At the reference mass of 131.46 t, vertical kinetic energy is approximately 65.7 kJ at 1 m/s and 263 kJ at 2 m/s. With no engine support and a total stopping stroke s, the minimum average total normal force is m[g + w²/(2s)], where w is the initial downward speed. Peak and single-leg forces may be larger, particularly when the feet contact at different times. Unknown leg stiffness, damping, stroke, friction, and ratings prevent these energy estimates from establishing contact feasibility.

before: Contact dynamics must impose unilateral normal force, friction/stick-slip behavior, finite compression stroke, and finite deck coverage. An equivalent spring-damper model may be a first approximation, but its deformation must represent a defined compliance, not permitted rigid-body penetration of the deck. At least two seconds after first contact should be checked for sliding, overturning, load, and compression under the assumed safety window.
after: A contact model must include unilateral normal forces, friction, a finite compression stroke, and finite deck coverage. A spring-damper approximation must represent a defined compliant component rather than allow unphysical penetration by the rigid vehicle. The assumed two-second post-contact window should be checked for sliding, overturning, support loads, and compression limits.

before: A simple upright, rigid, non-sliding pivot model gives a static tipping angle arctan(b/ℓ) ≈ 8.75° and a zero-thrust energy barrier near 493 kJ. The 2-degree contact limit alone is not a dynamic anti-tip certificate.
after: An upright rigid-body pivot model with zero thrust and no sliding gives a static tipping angle arctan(b/ℓ) ≈ 8.75° and a potential-energy barrier of approximately 493 kJ. Any dynamic use of that barrier must include initial rotational energy and external work. It does not establish stability for powered contact, compliant legs, or a moving deck; the 2° contact limit alone is likewise insufficient.

before: The candidate still has upward thrust near 0.950 times weight at its CG reference endpoint. Static normal support would then be only about 0.050 times weight if other forces were absent. Full mg must not be assumed when estimating available friction or restoring support. Under the same immediate-shutdown response model, the two-engine tail has approximately 386 kN s impulse and consumes about 123 kg, excluding any additional off-command delay or plume/ground effects. Thrust and body angular rate cannot simply be reset to zero at contact.
after: At the CG reference endpoint, upward thrust is approximately 0.950 times local weight. Static normal support would therefore be only about 0.050 times weight if other forces were absent, reducing the support available for friction. Under the same response model, an immediate off command produces a two-engine tail impulse of approximately 386 kN s and consumes about 123 kg. This excludes additional command delay and plume/deck interaction. Thrust and angular rate must evolve continuously through contact, rather than being reset to zero.

before: Dynamic pressure and force budget are useful screens, not structural or thermal ratings. Bending moment, local stress, buckling, flexible response, and propellant slosh depend on load distribution and mass properties. A stagnation-point scaling of the form q̇h ∝ √(ρ/Rn) V³ illustrates the separate sensitivity of heating to speed [11], but no heating coefficient, effective engine-end radius, heat shield, wall temperature, or allowable heat load has been established. Retropropulsion changes the flow and cannot be treated as a passive-body thermal correction without evidence [10]. Neither structural integrity nor reuse readiness is certified by q < 50 kPa.
after: Dynamic pressure and the force budget do not determine structural or thermal capacity. Bending, stress, buckling, flexible response, and propellant slosh require load distributions and mass properties. The stagnation-point scaling q̇h ∝ √(ρ/Rn) V³ illustrates the separate sensitivity of heating to speed [11], but no applicable heating coefficient, effective engine-end radius, thermal protection, or allowable temperature and heat load is established. Retropropulsion further changes the flow [10]. Passing q < 50 kPa therefore does not establish structural integrity or reuse readiness.

before: 10.1 Strengths of the approach
after: 10.1 Interpretation of the results

before: The approach has three useful features. First, variable mass is coupled to the trajectory rather than attached after a guessed velocity budget, so the propellant estimate is a genuine solution of the coupled equations rather than a post hoc rocket-equation insertion. Second, nominal solutions are checked by independent coordinate and integration implementations, which separates the physical result from any single solver artifact. Third, attitude and contact constraints are used to falsify overly strong safety claims, converting the underdetermination of the problem from a weakness into an explicit, auditable boundary.
after: The computation closes the propellant balance through the trajectory rather than applying the rocket equation to an assumed velocity budget. Independent integrations support the resulting nominal benchmark. The attitude analysis then identifies an incompatibility that numerical convergence cannot resolve: retaining the same translational path may require more net deflection than an assumed actuator can supply. A propellant estimate for complete recovery must therefore be based on a trajectory that passes both translational and rotational requirements.

before: The most important unresolved data are the initial flight-path angle, actual thrust and specific-impulse maps, consistent drag/lift/moment data, center-of-mass and inertia histories, actuator torque and deflection limits, landing-leg and deck properties, and structural/thermal capacities. The current study does not solve a robust closed-loop landing problem; it searches one schedule family through a limited initial-guess chain. It does not show that a different engine count, coast duration, aerodynamic design, or feedback strategy could not use less propellant. It also does not show that adding more propellant alone fixes the safety deficiencies: extra mass changes thrust-to-weight ratio and the trajectory.
after: The main unresolved inputs are the initial flight-path angle; thrust and specific-impulse maps; consistent aerodynamic forces and moments; center-of-mass and inertia histories; actuator limits; landing-leg and deck properties; and structural and thermal capacities. The search covers one strategy family and a limited warm-start path, not a robust closed-loop landing problem. Other engine counts, ignition times, aerodynamic designs, or feedback policies may change the required load. Adding propellant alone cannot be assumed to cure the deficiencies because it also changes thrust-to-weight ratio and the trajectory.

before: A logical completion sequence is to fix a supportable actuator and mass-property scenario, jointly optimize translation and rotation with force/moment allocation, introduce guidance feedback or receding-horizon replanning, validate fixed-ship disturbances, detect true foot and envelope contact, and simulate at least two seconds of support dynamics with structural and thermal checks. Propellant should then be compared among candidates that pass the same full set of requirements. Until then, 149 t is neither a verified feasible upper bound nor a rigorous lower bound for the complete safe-landing problem.
after: A complete estimate requires a specified actuator and mass-property scenario, joint translation–rotation optimization, feedback guidance, fixed-ship disturbance tests, actual foot and envelope contact events, and post-contact support, structural, and thermal checks. Candidates should then be compared under the same requirements. The present 149 t benchmark is neither a demonstrated feasible upper bound nor a rigorous lower bound for that complete problem.

before: 11.1 Summary of achievements
after: 11.1 Main findings

before: The problem's given quantities do not uniquely determine the required real propellant, because several decisive propulsion, trajectory, and safety specifications are absent. For an explicitly horizontal, wind-free, constant-drag, virtual-engine scenario, a reproducible M0 trajectory carries approximately 149 t of liquid oxygen and methane, consumes approximately 148 t, and reaches a CG reference endpoint after about 218 s at nominal downrange 206 km. Peak dynamic pressure is about 47.0 kPa, and the reference descent speed is approximately 1.00 m/s. The trajectory is supported by grid convergence to 0.0189%, independent Cartesian and polar coordinate agreement to below 10⁻⁴ m/s, and independent integrator agreement to below 10⁻⁵ m/s.
after: Under the stated horizontal, wind-free, constant-drag, virtual-engine assumptions, the selected M0 candidate carries 149.30 t of total propellant and consumes 147.84 t before reaching a CG reference height of 32.5 m. The flight lasts 217.75 s, ends at a downrange distance of 206.35 km, and has a peak dynamic pressure of 47.01 kPa and a reference descent speed of approximately 1.00 m/s. Refining the control grid from 160 to 320 intervals changes the initial load by 0.0189%. The radial endpoint differences are approximately 1.54×10⁻⁷ m/s between coordinate implementations and 1.05×10⁻⁵ m/s between DOP853 and RK45.

before: 11.2 What remains to be established
after: 11.2 Implications for recovery

before: This result answers a conditional numerical question, not the full safety question. Keeping the same trajectory requires a net thrust-to-body deflection of at least 24.8 degrees at one high-pressure instant; actual capability is unknown. Foot rotational velocities and non-simultaneous support matter, and nine deterministic perturbations fail the unchanged open-loop plan. The defensible outcome is a nominal propellant benchmark together with explicit conditions for a safe model, rather than an unsupported claim of safe recovery or minimum fuel.
after: These numerical checks support reproducibility, not complete recovery feasibility. Retaining the trajectory under the assumed high-pressure inflow constraint requires at least 24.8° net thrust-to-body deflection at one instant, and all nine deterministic perturbations fail the unchanged open-loop plan. Actual foot-contact and post-contact safety remain unverified. The defensible result is thus an approximately 149 t conditional benchmark and a set of unresolved recovery requirements, rather than a verified safe load or minimum-propellant solution.

11.4 Closing remarks

The methodological contribution generalizes beyond this particular booster. Distinguishing what is given, drawn from literature, assumed, and unestablished — and using attitude and contact conditions to falsify rather than assert safety — provides a template for any recovery estimate made under partial information. The value of the framework is that it reports precisely the confidence that the evidence supports, rather than silently filling gaps with unstated assumptions.
11.3 Broader implications

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 3 presents the physical scales and preliminary diagnostics. Section 4 develops the variable-mass translational model. Section 5 details the trajectory search and its independent acceptance. Section 6 reports the nominal trajectory and propellant result. Section 7 presents numerical verification and perturbation response. Section 8 derives the attitude feasibility conditions. Section 9 develops the foot-contact, deck-coverage, and post-contact safety checks. Section 10 discusses strengths, limitations, and a completion path, and Section 11 concludes.
